passages.t: No wife, no funeral, no feast
passages.happening:
The word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah: “You must not marry or have sons or daughters in this place” (verse 2). The children born in this land and their parents will die of deadly diseases, unmourned and unburied, finished by sword and famine (verses 3 and 4).

He must not enter a house where there is a funeral meal or go to mourn, for God has taken away his peace from this people, his loving devotion and compassion (verse 5). Great and small will die, and no one will bury or mourn them (verse 6). No one will share the bread or the cup of comfort with those who grieve for a father or mother (verse 7). He must not go into a house of feasting either (verse 8), for God will silence ‘the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom’ (verse 9).

When the people ask what their sin is (verse 10), Jeremiah is to answer that their fathers forsook the LORD and followed other gods (verse 11), and that they have done worse, each following the stubbornness of his evil heart (verse 12). So God will throw them into a land unknown to them, where they will serve other gods day and night (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Marriage and children were the ordinary expectation for an Israelite man, the way a family's name and land were carried on. An unmarried prophet would have stood out in a small town. That was the point. People would ask why, and his answer was the message.

The funeral meal was the food neighbors brought to a house of mourning, and the cup of comfort was shared with the bereaved. The mourning rites of verse 6 were customs the law had already forbidden to Israel, but the people practiced them. Jeremiah was to stay away from all of it, a living sign that soon there would be no one left to comfort anyone.

The chapter is undated, but it belongs to the years when Jeremiah was announcing the Babylonian conquest, probably under Jehoiakim. What it describes, death from famine and disease, unburied bodies and deportation, came to pass in the siege and fall of 588 to 586 BC.
passages.later: Paul also counsels some to stay unmarried ‘Because of the present crisis’ (1 Corinthians 7:26). Jeremiah 7 had already said God would silence ‘the voices of the bride and bridegroom’ (Jeremiah 7:34).
passages.hard:
Why would God forbid Jeremiah to marry, have children, or comfort the grieving?

These commands took from Jeremiah the ordinary goods of life, and they were meant to be seen. His empty house and his absence from funerals and weddings were a living sermon: soon families would be destroyed, mourning would be impossible, and joy would fall silent. Some readers also see mercy in the first command, since any wife and children he had would have faced the horrors of the siege. The ban on mourning did not mean God no longer cared about grief; the book elsewhere gives voice to grief over the people, at times as God's own word (9:1; 14:17).

The command was for Jeremiah in his time. Nothing in the text makes it a rule for anyone else, and it is no judgment on anyone who is single or without children. It shows that a calling can cost a person what everyone else takes for granted.
passages.asks: Jeremiah's life itself became the message. Ask what your life says without words. And ask what ordinary good you might be asked to give up for the sake of what God has called you to.

passages.t: A new exodus, and the nations come
passages.happening:
‘Yet behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD’ (verse 14). People will no longer swear by the God who brought Israel out of Egypt, but by the God who brought them back from the land of the north and all the lands where he banished them. He will bring them back to the land he gave their fathers (verses 14 and 15).

‘But for now I will send for many fishermen, declares the LORD, and they will catch them’ (verse 16). Then hunters will hunt them on every mountain and hill. ‘For My eyes are on all their ways’ (verse 17). He will repay them double for defiling his land with their idols (verse 18).

Jeremiah prays. ‘O LORD, my strength and my fortress, my refuge in the day of distress, the nations will come to You from the ends of the earth’ (verse 19). They will say their fathers inherited nothing but lies and worthless idols (verse 19). ‘Can man make gods for himself? Such are not gods’ (verse 20). And God says he will make them know his power and his might, ‘then they will know that My name is the LORD’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The exodus from Egypt was the great act of salvation by which Israel swore. Verse 14 says a new rescue, from the north, will be so great that people will swear by it instead.

That promise was first fulfilled in part after Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC and let the exiles go home. Jewish communities stayed scattered across many lands for centuries, which is one reason later Jewish and Christian readers kept looking for a fuller fulfillment.

The fishermen and hunters in verse 16 are a picture of judgment: no one can hide from the armies sent to find them. Before the return, the scattering.

The chapter ends with the nations coming to Israel's God and confessing that their own fathers worshiped lies. Even the dark book of Jeremiah holds that hope.
passages.later: Isaiah also says the new rescue will outshine the old: ‘Do not call to mind the former things’ (Isaiah 43:18). The law had forbidden the mourning rites of verse 6 to Israel (Deuteronomy 14:1).
passages.asks: God promised a rescue so great it would outshine the exodus. Ask what rescue in your own life you swear by, and whether you expect God to do something new. And ask what you have inherited that is only lies and worthless idols.
